lesson_title: Profit Up, Cash Down: Financial Statements and Cash Flow
hook_text: The company made R423 400 profit this year — and its bank balance went DOWN by R31 000. Both numbers are correct.
clip_script: Picture a family that runs a weekend market stall, sitting down in December to talk money. First question: how did the year go? That is the income statement — the whole year played back at speed, ending on one figure: R423 400 after tax. Second question: what do we own tonight? That is the balance sheet — one photograph at midnight on the last day, and both sides total R4 100 000, because nothing owned is unclaimed. Third question — the grade 12 question: where is the CASH? Because the family notices something odd. The playback says the year earned over four hundred thousand, yet the cashbox holds LESS than last December. Both statements are true at once. Profit counts a sale the day it happens, even if the customer pays in February. It spreads the cost of the gazebo over years. It counts a promised dividend nowhere at all. The cashbox counts only money. The cash flow statement is the bridge between the playback and the box — three strides: trading put R359 000 in, the company planted R550 000 in its own future, and the funders added R160 000. Open the box: down R31 000, to exactly R200 000 — the same figure in the photograph. When the bridge lands on the balance sheet's cash, every stride is proven.
visual_style: A market stall year on fast-forward collapsing into a single profit figure; a freeze-frame balance sheet splitting into owned and owed columns; then a three-plank bridge from the profit figure to a cashbox that opens on exactly R200 000.
pacing: Quick setup of the three questions, a beat of puzzlement on profit-up-cash-down, steady strides across the bridge, snap close on the matching figure.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build all three statements until they interlock.
